adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/scripts/spans/add-buffer.lua (zadd member = payload, ~line 45) — P1, confidence 75: Switching from set to sorted set keyed by raw payload bytes collapses byte-identical spans into one member; zadd silently overwrites (only updating score), so duplicate-but-distinct spans are silently dropped and zcard undercounts

adjudication.rationale: The diff changes Redis storage from SETs (SADD/SCARD/SSCAN/SUNIONSTORE) to sorted sets (ZADD/ZCARD/ZSCAN/ZUNIONSTORE) where the *member* is still the raw `span.payload` bytes (see `buffer.py` `p.zadd(set_key, {span.payload: span.end_timestamp_precise ...})` and `add-buffer.lua` `zunionstore`/`zcard`). However, the finding claims this switch newly causes byte-identical spans to collapse and be dropped; SETs already deduplicate identical members the same way (SADD also stores unique members and SCARD would also undercount duplicates). Nothing in the diff shows a new loss mode specific to ZADD beyond what already existed with SADD, and distinct spans are serialized into `payload.value` including `span_id` (and now `end_timestamp_precise`), so distinct spans should not be byte-identical by default.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/scripts/spans/add-buffer.lua (redirect loop 10000 → 1000, ~line 30) — P1, confidence 75: Lowering the redirect limit from 10000 to 1000 unconditionally lowers the depth ceiling 10×; deep traces break out of the loop with set_span_id pointing at an intermediate node, causing spans to attach to the wrong segment key with no error path

adjudication.rationale: In add-buffer.lua the redirect-follow loop cap is reduced from 10000 to 1000 (`for i = 0, 1000 do`). The loop resolves `set_span_id` by following `hget` redirects and breaks only when the chain ends (`not new_set_span`) or stabilizes. If a redirect chain exceeds 1000 hops, the loop will exit due to the iteration limit with `set_span_id` still pointing to an intermediate node, yet the script proceeds to `hset` the redirect (`hset ... span_id, set_span_id`) and merges span sets under `set_key` derived from that intermediate `set_span_id`, with no error/flag. This matches the finding: the depth ceiling is lowered 10× and can cause incorrect segment attachment for very deep redirect chains.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/scripts/spans/add-buffer.lua (eviction, ~lines 56–60) — P1, confidence 50: zpopmin on overflow evicts the lowest-end_timestamp_precise members — the oldest spans of a still-buffering trace — permanently deleting up to span_count - 1000 spans before flush without any metric or error, silently losing data for large traces and interacting badly with the span_count undercount issue

adjudication.rationale: In `src/sentry/scripts/spans/add-buffer.lua`, spans are now stored in a sorted set with score `end_timestamp_precise` (`zadd` in `buffer.py`), and when `span_count > 1000` the script executes `zpopmin(set_key, span_count - 1000)`. This deterministically removes the lowest-scored members, i.e., the oldest `end_timestamp_precise` spans, before any flush happens. There is no metric/log/error around this eviction, so large traces will silently lose spans. The finding’s core claim (silent data loss by evicting oldest spans on overflow) is directly supported by the diff; the mentioned “span_count undercount issue” isn’t clearly evidenced, but isn’t necessary for the data-loss conclusion.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/spans/consumers/process/factory.py:136 — P1, confidence 50: val["end_timestamp_precise"] is hard-required and any producer/older schema lacking it raises KeyError in process_batch, failing the whole batch; also a deployment/rollback hazard since mixed old-code sadd writes and new-code zset reads cause WRONGTYPE errors on zcard/zscan

adjudication.rationale: The diff makes `end_timestamp_precise` a required field in `process_batch` (`end_timestamp_precise=val["end_timestamp_precise"]`), so any message lacking that key will raise `KeyError` and fail batch processing. Separately, the diff changes the Redis data type for the same span buffer keys from Set to Sorted Set (`sadd`/`sscan`/`scard` -> `zadd`/`zscan`/`zcard` and Lua uses `zunionstore`), which creates a rolling deploy/rollback hazard: existing keys written by old code as Sets will trigger Redis `WRONGTYPE` errors when new code runs `zcard`/`zscan`/`zunionstore` on them.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/spans/buffer.py (_load_segment_data) — P2, confidence 75: Deleting the max_segment_spans guard leaves only the Lua-side 1000-member cap, which only applies at insert time; pre-existing set keys or zsets >1000 via union can exceed it, and set→zset transition causes WRONGTYPE errors on zcard/zscan at flush time with no migration handling

adjudication.rationale: The diff changes span buffer Redis storage from sets to sorted sets: `process_spans` now uses `zadd`, `_load_segment_data` uses `zscan`, and Lua `add-buffer.lua` now uses `zcard`/`zunionstore`/`zpopmin` instead of `scard`/`sunionstore`. There is no compatibility/migration handling for pre-existing keys that are still Redis SETs; calling `zadd`, `zcard`, or `zscan` on a SET will raise Redis WRONGTYPE, breaking ingestion/flush on upgrade. This is directly exposed by the diff. The part about exceeding 1000 via union is less certain because Lua caps after union, but the WRONGTYPE transition issue is a concrete defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: add-buffer.lua eviction (zpopmin when span_count > 1000) silently drops the oldest spans — those closest to being flushed — causing them to be permanently missing from the flushed segment tree; eviction should be tied to the flush lifecycle instead of dropping oldest pending spans

adjudication.rationale: In add-buffer.lua the new cap logic `if span_count > 1000 then redis.call("zpopmin", set_key, span_count - 1000) end` will silently evict ZSET members with the lowest score. Since the ZSET score is populated from `Span.end_timestamp_precise` (buffer.py uses `zadd(... {payload: span.end_timestamp_precise})`), this deterministically drops the earliest-timestamp spans whenever a segment exceeds 1000 buffered spans. That is a meaningful behavioral/design change (data is discarded rather than handled at flush time), but the diff alone doesn’t establish that keeping >1000 spans is required or that “closest to being flushed” is correct, so it’s hard to label as a definite defect vs an intended cap.

adjudication_records.issue_text: add-buffer.lua: zpopmin can pop span_count - 1000 members in a single blocking O(M·log N) call if a zunionstore merge jumps the cap, blocking the hot ingest path; should pop in bounded batches

adjudication.rationale: In add-buffer.lua, after potentially large zunionstore merges, the code enforces a cap with `redis.call("zpopmin", set_key, span_count - 1000)`. If `span_count` becomes much larger than 1000, this will remove a large number of members in a single Redis command, which is plausibly an O(M·log N) operation and could increase latency/blocking on a hot ingest script. This is a concrete, diff-grounded performance concern rather than a correctness defect (it still caps correctly).

adjudication_records.issue_text: buffer.py: removal of the max_segment_spans cap leaves only byte-based bounding; many tiny spans can accumulate an unbounded number of Python bytes objects in payloads[key], with memory several times the byte budget due to object overhead

adjudication.rationale: In `spans/buffer.py::_load_segment_data`, the diff removes the `max_segment_spans` guard that previously aborted when `len(payloads[key]) > self.max_segment_spans`. After switching from `sscan` to `zscan`, it now only checks `sizes[key] > self.max_segment_bytes` and then `payloads[key].extend(span for span, _ in zscan_values)` with no count-based cap. This makes the number of Python `bytes` objects accumulated in `payloads[key]` potentially very large when spans are tiny (byte budget grows slowly), increasing memory usage beyond the raw byte total due to per-object/list overhead.

adjudication_records.issue_text: OptimizedCursorPaginator: negative-offset slicing for prev cursors will raise Django's AssertionError 'Negative indexing is not supported'; the claimed Django negative-slice handling is false and the prev-handling trim condition using raw negative offset is dead/incorrect, so prev-cursor requests via the optimized_pagination path crash

adjudication.rationale: The new `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result` explicitly allows negative offsets when `enable_advanced_features` is true: `start_offset = cursor.offset` and then `results = list(queryset[start_offset:stop])` (with `start_offset < 0`). Django `QuerySet` slicing does not support negative indices and typically raises `AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported`, so the optimized path can crash if a cursor with a negative `offset` is supplied. This is reachable from `OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint.get` when `optimized_pagination=true` and the user is a superuser/global-access member (it passes `enable_advanced_features=True`). Additionally, later logic compares `len(results)` to `offset + limit + extra` using the raw (possibly negative) `offset`, which becomes nonsensical if negative offsets are used.

adjudication_records.issue_text: zadd keyed by payload collapses byte-identical spans to a single zset member, so real span counts can be lower than span_count implies and the flusher consumes fewer spans than were ingested, interacting with eviction/flush accounting

adjudication.rationale: In the diff, spans are stored in Redis under `set_key` as a collection keyed by the payload bytes: previously via `SADD` into a Redis Set, now via `ZADD` into a Redis Sorted Set (`buffer.py`: `p.zadd(set_key, {span.payload: span.end_timestamp_precise ...})`). Both Sets and Sorted Sets use the member as a unique key, so byte-identical payloads would have been deduplicated before as well. The finding claims this deduplication is newly introduced and causes the flusher to consume fewer spans than were ingested, but the same uniqueness property existed in the prior `SADD`/`SUNIONSTORE` approach. Nothing in the shown diff adds separate ingestion-count accounting that would now be violated by this behavior.

adjudication_records.issue_text: add-buffer.lua: lowering the redirect-loop bound from 10000 to 1000 makes deep-segment-tree silent join failure 10× more reachable and drops the acknowledgment comment, trading a rare correctness case for CPU bounding

adjudication.rationale: The diff in `add-buffer.lua` changes the redirect resolution loop from `for i = 0, 10000 do  -- ... depth 10k may not be joined ...` to `for i = 0, 1000 do` and removes the explanatory comment. This is a concrete behavior change that reduces the maximum redirect-chain depth that can be resolved before the loop stops, potentially making very deep chains fail to fully join. However, the diff alone doesn’t prove such depths occur or that the failure is definitively a new, user-visible defect (it was already bounded before), so it’s best framed as an edge-case/correctness-vs-CPU tradeoff concern rather than a clearly verifiable bug.

adjudication_records.issue_text: P0: Existing Redis buffers hold set-type keys; code now issues zset commands (zcard/zadd/zunionstore/zscan), causing WRONGTYPE errors during rolling deploy with no migration or TYPE check (add-buffer.lua:43-52, buffer.py:197)

adjudication.rationale: The diff changes the Redis data structure used for span buffers from Set to Sorted Set without any compatibility handling. In `add-buffer.lua`, `scard`/`sunionstore` are replaced with `zcard`/`zunionstore`, and in `buffer.py` `sadd`/`sscan` are replaced with `zadd`/`zscan`. If any existing `span-buf:s:{...}:...` keys were created by the old code as Redis Sets, the new ZSET commands against those keys will raise Redis `WRONGTYPE` errors during a rolling deploy, since no migration/TYPE check/fallback is shown in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: P0: Negative-offset slicing on a Django queryset raises AssertionError ('Negative indexing is not supported'), contradicting the comment's claim that Django ORM handles negative slicing; admins using ?optimized_pagination=true with negative-offset cursor get 500s (paginator.py OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result)

adjudication.rationale: In `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`, when `enable_advanced_features` is true and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code sets `start_offset = cursor.offset` and performs `queryset[start_offset:stop]` (negative start). Django QuerySet slicing does not support negative indices and will raise an `AssertionError` (“Negative indexing is not supported”), contradicting the in-code comment and causing a 500 if a negative-offset cursor is provided on the optimized path (`organization_auditlogs.py` passes `enable_advanced_features=True`).

adjudication_records.issue_text: P0: Required read of val["end_timestamp_precise"] on external ingest_spans_v1 events raises KeyError for events from producers/backlogged topics lacking the key, crashing batch processing instead of falling back to a default (factory.py:139)

adjudication.rationale: In `src/sentry/spans/consumers/process/factory.py`, the diff changes span construction to unconditionally read `end_timestamp_precise=val["end_timestamp_precise"]` after `rapidjson.loads(payload.value)`. Since `val` is a parsed dict-like payload and the code does not use `.get()` or provide a default, any message lacking this key will raise `KeyError` and can crash batch processing. The diff itself shows no validation/compat handling and updates tests to always include the field, reinforcing that absence is not handled.

adjudication_records.issue_text: P1: Span NamedTuple gained required field end_timestamp_precise inserted before is_segment_span, silently shifting positional arguments and causing missing-argument TypeErrors in call sites not updated; public signature of shared type changed with no deprecation (buffer.py:119)

adjudication.rationale: The diff does add a new required field `end_timestamp_precise: float` to the `Span(NamedTuple)` in `src/sentry/spans/buffer.py`, inserted before `is_segment_span` (previously last with a default). This changes the positional argument order and makes construction without that field invalid, which is a real API/compatibility hazard for any call sites using positional args or not updated to pass the new required field. However, within the shown diff, the visible constructions are updated and/or use keyword arguments, so the claim that it is already causing missing-argument `TypeError`s in unupdated call sites cannot be directly verified from this diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: P1: zpopmin in add-buffer.lua silently evicts oldest spans once count > 1000, replacing the previous skip-wholesale behavior with error metric segment_span_count_exceeded; flushed segments arrive incomplete to downstream consumers with no error signal (add-buffer.lua:57-60)

adjudication.rationale: The diff changes span buffering from Redis sets to sorted sets and introduces a hard cap of 1000 items per set via `zpopmin` in `add-buffer.lua` (`if span_count > 1000 then ... zpopmin ... end`), which will drop spans (lowest score = oldest `end_timestamp_precise`) without any metric/log signal. At the same time, `SpansBuffer._load_segment_data` removes the prior guard that detected and skipped oversized segments with `metrics.incr("spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded")` and an error log. This makes it verifiable that oversized segments now get silently truncated rather than being rejected with an explicit error signal, leading to incomplete flushed segments downstream.

adjudication_records.issue_text: P2: sunionstore→zunionstore switch means byte-identical payload members collapse in a zset, silently dropping duplicate spans the set-based version kept (add-buffer.lua:45-52)

adjudication.rationale: The diff switches span storage from Redis sets to sorted sets (e.g., buffer.py: `sadd`→`zadd`, add-buffer.lua: `sunionstore`→`zunionstore`). However, Redis Sets already de-duplicate members by value, so the prior set-based implementation would also collapse byte-identical payloads. A ZSET likewise stores unique members (payload bytes) and would not newly introduce duplicate-dropping behavior compared to SETs; it only changes the associated score (`end_timestamp_precise`) and ordering/capping behavior.

adjudication_records.issue_text: P2: Redirect-chain depth limit silently reduced from 10000 to 1000, causing deep segment trees (>1000) to break out early and attach spans to intermediate parents with no feature flag or migration note (add-buffer.lua:30)

adjudication.rationale: The diff in `src/sentry/scripts/spans/add-buffer.lua` changes the redirect-chain traversal loop from `for i = 0, 10000 do` (with a comment acknowledging deep chains) to `for i = 0, 1000 do` with no other compensating logic. Since the loop determines the final `set_span_id` used for `hset(main_redirect_key, span_id, set_span_id)`, any redirect chain longer than 1000 will stop before reaching its terminal/root mapping and will use an intermediate `set_span_id`, changing/breaking span attachment behavior for deep trees.

adjudication_records.issue_text: P2: New opt-in optimized_pagination param switches paginator classes with different cursor/hits semantics, so cursors minted under one mode are invalid under the other and Link header/cursor compatibility is not preserved (organization_auditlogs.py:68-88)

adjudication.rationale: The endpoint now conditionally switches paginator implementations based on a query param (`optimized_pagination`) and privileges (organization_auditlogs.py). Since the paginator class is part of how cursors are interpreted/minted, a cursor generated in one mode may not be usable if the client (or the server-provided Link header) does not consistently preserve `optimized_pagination=true` on subsequent requests. The diff does not show any explicit preservation of this param in generated pagination links, so cursor compatibility across modes is a concrete API-contract concern, though not provably broken from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: P2: Clamping negative offsets via max(0, offset) in shared BasePaginator.get_result changes behavior for all paginators, silently returning from offset 0 for malformed negative-offset cursors instead of erroring and masking client bugs (paginator.py:180-183)

adjudication.rationale: In `src/sentry/api/paginator.py` the shared `get_result` logic now uses `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` before slicing. This will change behavior for non-`is_prev` cursors with a negative `cursor.offset`: instead of Django likely raising on negative queryset slicing (or otherwise behaving differently), it will silently clamp to `0` and return results from the beginning. That’s a real, diff-grounded behavioral change that could mask malformed cursors/client bugs, but it only affects invalid/edge input and is framed as an optimization in comments, so it’s better categorized as a non-bug review concern rather than a definite defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: P0: Redis key format migration not handled — existing set-typed keys will raise WRONGTYPE under zcard/zscan after the switch to sorted sets, with no migration path or versioned key naming

adjudication.rationale: The diff switches span buffer storage from Redis Sets to Sorted Sets but keeps the same key names (e.g. `span-buf:s:{...}:{...}` in `buffer.py` and `add-buffer.lua`). Python now writes with `zadd` and reads with `zscan`, and Lua now uses `zcard`/`zunionstore`/`zpopmin`. Any pre-existing keys of the same name created by the previous `sadd`/`sscan` implementation would remain type `set`, causing Redis `WRONGTYPE` errors when the new code executes `zcard`/`zscan`/`zunionstore` against them. The diff shows no versioned key naming, cleanup, or migration handling to avoid this.

adjudication_records.issue_text: P1: Eviction via zpopmin can silently drop structural spans (root/parent/segment) needed by tree-joining logic, and the eviction path has zero test coverage

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds an eviction path in `add-buffer.lua` that unconditionally trims any merged span set to 1000 members using `zpopmin(set_key, span_count - 1000)`. Since scores are `end_timestamp_precise` (from `buffer.py` `zadd(..., {payload: end_timestamp_precise})`), this will drop the lowest-score (earliest-ending) spans without regard to whether they are structurally important (e.g., segment/root/parent spans needed to correctly reconstruct the tree). Previously, `buffer.py` enforced an oversize guard by skipping segments when span counts exceeded `max_segment_spans`; that safety check was removed, so the system may now flush partially-truncated segments. No tests in the diff exercise or assert behavior around this new eviction/truncation path.

adjudication_records.issue_text: P1: max_segment_spans guard removed from flusher with no replacement backstop and no test coverage, allowing oversized segments to be flushed unbounded

adjudication.rationale: The diff removes the span-count backstop in `SpansBuffer._load_segment_data` (the `if len(payloads[key]) > self.max_segment_spans: ... skip` block is deleted) and replaces `sscan` with `zscan` without any equivalent count-based abort in the loader. While `add-buffer.lua` now caps merged sorted-sets to 1000 via `zpopmin`, the Python ingestion path (`process_spans` uses `p.zadd(...)`) does not enforce `max_segment_spans`, so a zset can still grow beyond the intended span-count limit (bounded only by `max_segment_bytes`). This can allow oversized segments (by count) to be loaded/flushed where they were previously rejected.

adjudication_records.issue_text: P2: Removed max_segment_spans guard in spans/buffer.py leaves only byte-size protection, allowing unbounded memory growth for segments with many tiny spans; or the config field/metrics become dead code

adjudication.rationale: The diff does remove the `max_segment_spans` enforcement in `SpansBuffer._load_segment_data`: the block that checked `if len(payloads[key]) > self.max_segment_spans` and then dropped the segment/raised metrics is deleted, leaving only the byte-size guard (`if sizes[key] > self.max_segment_bytes`). That means span-count is no longer bounded at load/flush time. However, the finding’s claim of “unbounded memory growth” isn’t fully verifiable from the diff because (a) there is still a byte-size cap, and (b) the Lua script now caps merged sorted sets to 1000 members (`zpopmin`), though it’s unclear if all writes go through that path (Python `zadd` doesn’t enforce a cap). So the core issue (span-count guard removed / potential dead config+metrics) is real, but the worst-case consequence is not conclusively proven here.

adjudication_records.issue_text: P2: Redirect-chain loop limit cut from 10k to 1000 in add-buffer.lua without metric, log, or fallback, so deep segment trees will silently fail to join

adjudication.rationale: In `src/sentry/scripts/spans/add-buffer.lua`, the redirect-resolution loop cap is reduced from `for i = 0, 10000 do` to `for i = 0, 1000 do`. The loop only `break`s when `hget` returns nil or the same id; if the redirect chain is longer than the cap, the loop will terminate due to the `for` bound without any error/metric and proceed to `hset`/union using a non-final `set_span_id`. That can leave long redirect chains partially unresolved and thus prevent full joining of deep segment trees, and it happens silently in the script as shown in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: P2: Switching sadd to zadd with zunionstore default AGGREGATE SUM causes duplicate members' scores to be summed across passes, yielding meaningless scores that corrupt zpopmin eviction ordering; should use AGGREGATE MAX

adjudication.rationale: In `add-buffer.lua`, the code now stores spans in sorted sets with `zadd(..., score=end_timestamp_precise)` and merges sets via `zunionstore(set_key, 2, set_key, span_key)` / `zunionstore(set_key, 2, set_key, parent_key)` without specifying an `AGGREGATE`. Redis `ZUNIONSTORE` defaults to `AGGREGATE SUM`, so if the same span payload (member) exists in both inputs (or is merged repeatedly across passes), its timestamp score will be summed, producing incorrect scores. Since eviction later uses `zpopmin` based on these scores, distorted scores can corrupt eviction ordering/retention behavior.

adjudication_records.issue_text: P0: Silent span eviction — `zpopmin` in add-buffer.lua permanently deletes oldest spans from segments exceeding 1000 members before they are ever flushed, with no metric, log, or caller signal, causing silent data loss

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds an unconditional hard cap in `add-buffer.lua`: after building/merging the sorted-set segment (`set_key`), it computes `span_count` and if `span_count > 1000` it executes `redis.call("zpopmin", set_key, span_count - 1000)`, which permanently removes the lowest-score (oldest by `end_timestamp_precise`) spans from the buffer. There is no metric/log/caller-visible signal in the Lua script when this eviction happens. Since the buffer flush path in `spans/buffer.py` now reads spans via `zscan` from these same keys, any popped spans are lost before they can be flushed, matching the finding’s "silent data loss" claim.

adjudication_records.issue_text: P1: Redirect chain depth limit silently reduced from 10000 to 1000, so longer chains exit the loop pointing at an intermediate node and spans are inserted into the wrong segment set or orphaned, silently fragmenting traces (add-buffer.lua loop bound)

adjudication.rationale: In `add-buffer.lua`, the redirect resolution loop bound is reduced from `for i = 0, 10000 do` to `for i = 0, 1000 do` with no added detection/handling for hitting the limit. The loop updates `set_span_id` as it follows `hget` redirects and only stops early on `not new_set_span` or `new_set_span == set_span_id`. If a redirect chain exceeds 1000 (1001 iterations inclusive), the loop will terminate due to the bound and leave `set_span_id` pointing to an intermediate node, after which the script `hset`s `span_id` -> `set_span_id` and unions data into that set. This matches the finding that long chains can be silently truncated and cause spans to be associated with the wrong segment key (trace fragmentation/orphaning).

adjudication_records.issue_text: P1: Client-controlled negative cursor offsets flow into `queryset[start_offset:stop]` and trigger Django's AssertionError on negative slicing, causing a 500; the claim that Django ORM handles negative slicing is false (paginator.py OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result; cursors.py)

adjudication.rationale: The diff explicitly introduces code paths that can slice a Django QuerySet with a negative start index. In `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`, when `enable_advanced_features` is true and `cursor.offset < 0`, it sets `start_offset = cursor.offset` and does `queryset[start_offset:stop]`. Django QuerySet slicing with a negative start raises `AssertionError` (negative indexing not supported), so this can produce a 500. Additionally, the earlier change to the existing paginator logic (`start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset`) still allows a negative `offset` through when `cursor.is_prev` is true. `Cursor.offset` is taken directly as `int(offset)` in `utils/cursors.py` with no validation/clamping, so a request-provided cursor can carry a negative offset into these slices (at least for users who can enable the optimized path). The inline comments claiming Django handles negative slicing are contradicted by Django behavior.
